transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-03-03 16:00 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Rina Patel (Redwood Solutions), Samir Patel (Lyric CTO), Jenna Lowe (Platform Eng), Marcus Green (ML Infra), Aisha Khan (Product)

Summary: quick discovery to size a pilot for high-concurrency streaming inference (tokenstorm scenario). Focus on p95 latency targets for 1k concurrent streams, fallback strategies, hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, and how to run token/sec benchmarks.

Topics: p95 targets, streaming concurrency, token/sec benchmarking, burst handling, KV/prefix cache, network egress, security (SAML/KMS), rollout plan.

--- Transcript body ---
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate you carving time. I'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Diego on the SE side. Can you each do a quick intro?
[00:00:08] Samir Patel: Yeah hi, Samir here, CTO at Lyric Analytics. We do real-time summarization and entity extraction for streaming transcripts — big spikes during events.
[00:00:13] Jenna Lowe: Jenna, platform eng. I run their k8s infra and we're responsible for inference pipeline.
[00:00:18] Marcus Green: Marcus, ML infra, I handle model infra and perf.
[00:00:21] Diego Alvarez: Great to meet you all. Quick note — we'll focus on p95 SLOs and the token throughput picture, not trying to sell, more figure out sizing.
[00:00:28] Samir: Perfect. So high level — we have typical background load ~200 streams, spikes to 1,200 concurrent during events. Each stream averages 40 tokens/sec while active, with intermittent bursts when a speaker talks. Our target p95 for end-to-end streaming response is 350ms. Does that make sense?
[00:00:44] Maya: 350ms p95 end-to-end, okay. Is that per partial chunk or for final message after 1-2 tokens?
[00:00:49] Samir: It's for streaming deltas — so the partial token latencies matter. We can tolerate slightly higher for long-form completions but prefer sub-350ms for the steady stream.
[00:00:56] Jenna: Also, we are constrained on egress and would prefer regional routing, ideally EU for EU customers.
[00:01:02] Diego: Noted. Two immediate buckets for us: 1) latency-critical streaming where partial tokens must come fast, 2) higher throughput rarer jobs where cost matters more. We'll talk about tradeoffs across Hosted / Dedicated / Private.
[00:01:12] [00:01:12] Marcus: Quick Q — our model is a 7B variant, quantized to int8, KV cache present. We also run a reranker on short contexts; can Redwood use the KV cache and keep warm sessions?
[00:01:24] Diego: Yes, continuous KV caching with sticky sessions is supported for Dedicated and Private; hosted also supports prefix caching but with more conservative retention depending on tenancy. For your 1,200 concurrent streams, caching will save tokens but you still need sufficient concurrency headroom.
[00:01:39] Samir: Okay, what's the typical tokens/sec per GPU baseline for a 7B int8 model on your stack? We want to map that to machines and cost.
[00:01:47] Diego: It varies with sequence length and optimized kernels. For short streaming deltas (~16 tokens windows) we often see effective throughput around 6k–10k tokens/sec per A100-class GPU when optimized for streaming, but p95 latency depends on batching. If you force strict single-request low-latency, that drops to 2k–4k tokens/sec per GPU.
[00:02:03] Jenna: So if we have 1,200 streams at 40 tokens/sec steady, that's 48k tokens/sec aggregate — rough math says we'd need 5–8 GPUs if we can achieve 6–10k/TPS, but with headroom for bursts maybe more.
[00:02:18] Diego: Exactly, and bursts matter — your peak may be 4× average. We recommend capacity planning for p95 during a 95th percentile burst profile. That usually means planning for ~2.5–3× baseline depending on KV hit rate.
[00:02:28] [00:02:28] Samir: Hmm, we don't have a precise burst multiple yet but 3× seems realistic.
[00:02:32] Maya: Let me pause — high level tradeoffs: Hosted gives fastest onboarding and cost elasticity but multi-tenant cache retention limits may increase token consumption. Dedicated gives reserved GPUs, predictable throughput, sticky KV caches, and custom batching. Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you total control for SSO/KMS and data residency but requires ops. Which way are you leaning?
[00:02:50] Samir: For the pilot, we prefer hosted to move quick, but if economics don't work we'll consider Dedicated. Private is last resort because of onboarding time.
[00:02:57] Marcus: Important: p95 SLA we need to show to customer-facing teams so predictability matters. Can Redwood provide p95 latency numbers for a dedicated pool?
[00:03:06] Diego: Yes, we can provide curated perf profiles. For a Dedicated A100 pool running your 7B int8 with streaming optimizations, 95th token latency for 16-token steps can be sub-200ms at modest concurrency per model instance. But with 1,200 concurrent streams, you'll be spreading across instances, so p95 will reflect cross-instance variance and networking.
[00:03:24] Jenna: About networking — we prefer a regional endpoint in eu-west and want egress cost estimations.
[00:03:29] Maya: We'll include egress estimates in the pricing sheet for the pilot.
[00:03:32] [00:03:32] Aisha Khan: One more question on fallbacks — if a model variant is saturated, can we automatically fail to a cheaper quantized model and preserve latency?
[00:03:40] Diego: Yes, Redwood's smart routing supports fallback policies: you can define routing by latency tier and cost tier; when primary is constrained it routes to a compatible variant. We also have graceful degraded responses and partial streaming if full model isn't available. There is some config to control quality thresholds.
[00:03:53] Samir: Good. We also need audit logs and KMS integration for data retention rules.
[00:03:58] Maya: We support KMS for Private and Dedicated, hosted has managed key options and SOC2 logs — we'll share the security brief.
[00:04:04] [00:04:04] Marcus: Diego, could you walk us through how you'd run an in-house token/sec benchmark? We want to reproduce your numbers.
[00:04:10] Diego: Sure — typical benchmark steps: 1) use a representative corpus: a mix of short partials and longer completions; 2) emulate sticky sessions to exercise KV cache; 3) run a ramp test with constant concurrency and also poisson bursts; 4) measure per-token latency distributions and effective tokens/sec. I'll share a repo with scripts and a Jupyter notebook.
[00:04:28] Jenna: Do you provide a loader to replay real traffic traces?
[00:04:31] Diego: We have a small harness and example k6 load tests. We'll attach them. For hosted pilots we can also run a benchmark in our sandbox region and share results.
[00:04:39] Samir: About canary/rollouts: if we start with hosted pilot and then move to Dedicated, what's the migration path?
[00:04:45] Maya: The API surface is the same, you can pin model versions and switch routing to a Dedicated pool. We support canary splits and A/B testing and automatic fallback. We can support traffic mirroring too for shadow testing.
[00:04:55] [00:04:55] Aisha: Any constraints with session affinity across regions? If a user's stream started in EU and crosses to US region during a call...
[00:05:02] Diego: Cross-region affinity isn't ideal; we'd recommend session stickiness to the original region or a global front-door that proxies to the correct regional pool. Cross-region fallbacks add latency.
[00:05:10] Marcus: Cost question — can you give an order-of-magnitude hourly GPU cost for Dedicated and how that translates to per-token unit?
[00:05:16] Maya: We'll share precise numbers in the pricing sheet, but rough rule: a dedicated A100-class GPU runs you into mid-three digits per hour on reserved pricing in our pricing model; per-token depends on model size, cache hit rates, and batching; for heavy streaming optimized workloads with high cache hits you can approach low fractions of a cent per 1k tokens.
[00:05:33] Samir: Alright. We care a lot about p95 under burst — can Redwood run a benchmark that reproduces our 1,200 concurrent, 3× burst profile?
[00:05:39] Diego: Yes, if you provide a 48h traffic capture and sample prompts we'll run an equivalence benchmark in our sandbox and produce p50/p95/p99 numbers and token/sec. That will also drive an initial Dedicated sizing estimate.
[00:05:50] [00:05:50] Jenna: What metrics do we need to collect on our side to make this accurate?
[00:05:54] Diego: Ideally: timestamped request traces, session IDs, token counts per request, distribution of sequence lengths, and your observed KV hit rate. If you don't have KV hit rate, provide representative prompts so we can simulate.
[00:06:06] Samir: We can extract logs, but privacy wise we need guidance on redaction.
[00:06:10] Maya: We'll provide an upload checklist and a secure S3 link with instructions for redaction. For the pilot we can also accept synthetic equivalents.
[00:06:18] Aisha: Okay, timeline — we want a pilot by mid-April. Is that feasible?
[00:06:22] Maya: Yes, a two-week hosted pilot plus a week of benchmarking can fit that window. We'll need the trace and prompts early.
[00:06:28] [00:06:28] Marcus: Any gotchas for streaming partial token latencies we should be aware of?
[00:06:32] Diego: A few: client-side buffering, network TCP windowing, TLS handshake overhead for many tiny streams, batching heuristics in the runtime — if each stream sends tiny single-token requests you pay overhead. Aggregating partials into slightly larger chunks (e.g., 8–16 tokens) usually improves p95 for the same cost. Also keep an eye on cold-starts for KV — warm sessions help.
[00:06:53] Jenna: That aligns with our suspicions, we may adjust the client.
[00:06:56] Samir: Will Redwood help with client changes?
[00:06:59] Diego: Absolutely, we'll provide sample client logic for efficient partial flushing and retry/backoff patterns.
[00:07:05] Maya: Quick recap before we wrap: 1) Redwood will send pilot pricing + egress estimates, 2) Diego sends benchmark harness + runbook, 3) Jenna uploads 48h traffic trace + sample prompts, 4) Redwood runs sandbox benchmark and returns p50/p95/p99 and recommended Dedicated sizing. Any other asks?
[00:07:21] Aisha: Please include fallbacks and routing policy examples in the doc.
[00:07:25] Maya: Will do.
[00:07:27] [00:07:27] Samir: Thanks folks. One small nit — can you include an estimator for cost if we need to keep 30% headroom for bursts?
[00:07:35] Diego: Yes we will include a headroom multiplier in the sizing sheet.
[00:07:38] Jenna: Great. We'll follow up after we upload the trace.
[00:07:42] Maya: Thanks everyone, follow up email with links and next steps shortly.
[00:07:46] [crosstalk] Everyone: Thanks, bye.
